Welcome — thanks for stopping by. I wanted the first post here to be
about something I keep thinking about as a vet, a wildlife disease
ecologist, and someone who grew up in Southeast Asia: the places
where people, wild animals, and pathogens are pushed closer
together, and how often that push is something we do to ourselves.

## The pangolin on the cover

The most-trafficked wild mammal on Earth is almost certainly a
pangolin. All eight species — four in Africa, four in Asia, including
the **Sunda pangolin** (*Manis javanica*) across the region I come
from — are listed on CITES Appendix I, and all eight are in some
shade of red on the IUCN list. Their scales, made of the same keratin
as my fingernails, are smuggled by the tonne into traditional-medicine
markets. Their meat is a luxury dish. Estimates from seizure data
suggest **more than a million pangolins** have been pulled out of the
wild over the last two decades, and every estimate people bother to
make turns out to be an undercount.

That number matters beyond the animals themselves. Pangolins became
household names in 2020 when their role in the early SARS-CoV-2
investigation put them briefly on every front page. I don't think
pangolins caused that pandemic. But the episode made something
visible that wildlife veterinarians had been quietly writing about
for years: **illegally traded wildlife is a moving buffet of
pathogens**, carried through live-animal markets, back-road holding
pens, airport baggage, and courier networks that no diagnostic lab
has standing access to.

## Tracking wildlife in Southeast Asia

Part of why this is so hard to manage is that we have a very uneven
picture of what's moving around. My own work has been on the
*resident* side of that picture — GPS collars on gaur and banteng,
habitat-suitability models across thirteen Asian countries, stochastic
disease models that ask *what happens if a cattle-borne pathogen
actually meets a wild bovid population*.

A couple of things you learn quickly from that kind of tracking work:

- Wild bovid habitat in Southeast Asia is **fragmented and squeezed
  up against the working landscape**. Over half of the habitat that
  is still ecologically suitable for gaur, banteng, and wild water
  buffalo sits outside protected areas. That isn't a failure of
  conservation; it's a description of a continent where national
  parks are islands in a sea of agriculture, plantation, and human
  settlement.
- Where wild bovid habitat and domestic cattle density overlap, you
  get **interface zones** — forest edges, cropland borders, shared
  water points — that are exactly the kinds of places where
  pathogens like foot-and-mouth disease, haemorrhagic septicaemia,
  or brucellosis can move in either direction.
- Illegal hunting, snaring, and wildlife trafficking cut right
  through these same zones. So the same corridors that matter for
  conservation are also the corridors that matter for pathogen
  movement and for the wildlife trade.

It is, in other words, one landscape with several problems stacked on
top of each other.

## Land-use change is a disease driver

Most of the big emerging infectious disease events of the last fifty
years — **Nipah, SARS, MERS, Ebola, highly pathogenic avian
influenza, monkeypox/mpox, SARS-CoV-2** — share a pattern. A
pathogen that was quietly circulating in a wild host encountered
humans (or human-adjacent animals like pigs, poultry, civets, or
camels) because the edge between *wild* and *not-wild* shifted. A
forest was cleared, a plantation was expanded, a cave was mined, a
live-animal market scaled up, a trade route opened.

The published evidence on this has become hard to argue with.
Ecological studies show that **deforestation and landscape
fragmentation correlate with increases in zoonotic disease spillover
events**, because they change which animals live where, which
pathogens they carry, and how often any of that touches a human
community. The wildlife trade amplifies the effect — it takes that
edge and moves it, physically, into airports and cities.

The implication for my field is uncomfortable and, I think, freeing:
surveillance designed around known pathogens and known hosts will
always be chasing the last outbreak. Surveillance designed around the
**interfaces** — forest edges being cleared, markets that handle wild
species, transport chains that aggregate animals — has a chance of
catching the next one.

## One Health, honestly

"One Health" gets used so often in grant applications that it can
start to sound like a polite slogan. I want to try to keep it concrete
on this blog. For me, One Health means at least three things:

- **Shared data and shared surveillance.** Human, animal, and
  environmental health agencies in most of Southeast Asia (and most
  of the world) still track their own subsets of the picture in
  their own systems. The useful work is often the boring work of
  getting those datasets to speak to each other.
- **Conservation as disease prevention.** Keeping forests standing,
  keeping wild populations viable, and enforcing wildlife-trade
  regulations aren't separate from pandemic preparedness — they
  *are* pandemic preparedness, delivered upstream. The pangolin that
  stays in the forest doesn't enter a supply chain.
- **Field-first, lab-second.** The most important questions are
  almost never answered by a sample alone. They're answered by
  someone who has actually stood in the farm, the forest edge, or
  the market, and can tell you what "normal" looks like there.

## What I want to write about here

Expect short, unhurried pieces on:

- Wildlife conservation and illegal wildlife trade in Southeast Asia
- Emerging infectious diseases and what the underlying ecology is
  actually telling us
- Honest notes on using R and reproducible workflows for movement
  ecology, spatial epidemiology, and disease modelling
